questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.1 Class A airspace characteristics and sUAS prohibition
questions.keyword: Class A airspace FL180 sUAS operations
questions.text: A remote pilot is reviewing the U.S. airspace classification system and wants to understand Class A airspace. Under 14 CFR Part 71, Class A airspace begins at what altitude and continues upward, and how does it affect standard Part 107 sUAS operations?

answers.text: Class A begins at 18,000 ft MSL; standard Part 107 sUAS operations are already constrained well below this altitude and would never reach Class A
Class A begins at 10,000 ft MSL; sUAS may operate in Class A without authorization if they stay below 12,500 ft MSL
Class A begins at 14,500 ft MSL; sUAS need ATC authorization but may otherwise operate using standard VFR procedures
Class A begins at 18,000 ft MSL; sUAS may freely transit Class A airspace because it is above all controlled airport traffic areas

explanations.a: Class A airspace begins at 18,000 ft MSL and extends upward to FL600; because Part 107 limits sUAS to 400 ft AGL under standard rules, sUAS operations never approach Class A.
explanations.b: Class A begins at 18,000 ft MSL, not 10,000 ft; the 10,000 ft figure relates to Mode C transponder requirements for manned aircraft.
explanations.c: 14,500 ft MSL is not the Class A floor; the floor is 18,000 ft MSL and sUAS standard operations are nowhere near that altitude.
explanations.d: Class A begins at 18,000 ft MSL — the first part is correct — but sUAS do not freely operate in Class A; it is IFR-only airspace that sUAS cannot reach under standard Part 107 limits.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.2 Class B airspace structure and sUAS authorization requirement
questions.keyword: Class B authorization requirement sUAS
questions.text: A remote pilot wants to conduct a commercial photography flight near a major international airport. The sectional chart shows the proposed operating area is within Class B airspace. Under 14 CFR Part 107, what must the remote PIC obtain before flying in this airspace?

answers.text: ATC authorization from the controlling facility, obtainable via LAANC or FAA DroneZone prior to the operation
No authorization is needed because sUAS weigh less than 55 pounds and pose minimal risk to commercial aircraft at ground level
A written letter of agreement between the remote pilot and the airport authority governing the specific operation
A Class B airspace waiver filed with the FAA at least 90 days before the intended flight date

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR 107.41, no person may operate an sUAS in Class B airspace without ATC authorization; LAANC or the FAA DroneZone portal are the standard methods for obtaining this authorization.
explanations.b: Weight-based risk arguments do not substitute for the ATC authorization required to operate in Class B airspace; the authorization requirement applies regardless of aircraft size.
explanations.c: A letter of agreement with airport authority is not the regulatory authorization mechanism under Part 107; LAANC and DroneZone are the designated pathways.
explanations.d: There is no 90-day Class B waiver process for sUAS; airspace authorization through LAANC can often be obtained in seconds, while DroneZone applications take longer but are not the waiver process.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.2 Class B airspace structure and sUAS authorization requirement
questions.keyword: Class B upside-down wedding cake structure
questions.text: When reviewing a sectional chart near a major hub airport, a remote pilot notices concentric circles with different floor and ceiling altitudes surrounding the airport. These circles represent the layers of Class B airspace. How is the typical Class B airspace structure best described?

answers.text: A single large circle of uniform floor and ceiling altitude extending 20 nautical miles from the primary airport
A cylinder extending from the surface to 2,500 ft AGL within a 5-mile radius of the primary airport
A rectangular block of airspace centered on the airport with uniform dimensions up to 10,000 ft MSL
An inverted wedding cake with floors that rise with increasing distance from the airport, forming increasingly higher tiers

explanations.a: Class B is not a single uniform circle; it has multiple tiers with different floor and ceiling altitudes at different distances.
explanations.b: A uniform cylinder to 2,500 ft AGL describes a basic airport traffic area concept, not Class B; Class B typically extends from the surface or a defined floor to 10,000 ft MSL.
explanations.c: Class B is not a rectangular block and does not have uniform dimensions; it consists of concentric circles with varying floor and ceiling altitudes.
explanations.d: Class B airspace is described as resembling an inverted wedding cake, with successive tiers having higher floors as distance from the primary airport increases, allowing arriving and departing traffic to transition in and out.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.3 Class C airspace dimensions and services
questions.keyword: Class C airspace 5 nm inner ring surface
questions.text: A remote pilot wants to fly within the inner ring of Class C airspace surrounding a radar-equipped airport with an operational control tower and approach control. The sectional chart shows magenta circles representing the Class C airspace. What are the typical dimensions of the inner Class C ring?

answers.text: The inner ring extends from the surface to 4,000 ft AGL within a 5 nautical mile radius of the primary airport
The inner ring extends from the surface to 2,500 ft AGL within a 10 nautical mile radius of the primary airport
The inner ring extends from 1,200 ft AGL to 4,000 ft AGL within a 5 nautical mile radius of the primary airport
The inner ring extends from the surface to 2,500 ft AGL within a 5 nautical mile radius of the primary airport

explanations.a: The inner ring ceiling is 4,000 ft AGL above the primary airport elevation, but the inner ring radius is 5 nm from the surface — there is no 4,000 ft ceiling paired with a 5 nm inner ring in standard Class C.
explanations.b: The inner ring radius is 5 nm, not 10 nm; the outer shelf extends to approximately 10 nm.
explanations.c: Class C inner ring begins at the surface, not at 1,200 ft AGL; the surface-based portion is the core of Class C protection.
explanations.d: Standard Class C airspace has an inner ring extending from the surface to 4,000 ft above the primary airport elevation within a 5 nm radius; at many airports the ceiling is described as surface to 4,000 ft, but the floor-to-surface inner ring is the key point and the 5 nm radius is standard.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.3 Class C airspace dimensions and services
questions.keyword: Class C outer ring floor 1200 AGL
questions.text: Studying a sectional chart, a remote pilot identifies the outer ring of a Class C airspace shelf. The chart notation shows 40/12 for this ring. What does this notation indicate about the outer Class C shelf?

answers.text: The ceiling is 40 ft AGL and the floor begins at 12 ft AGL, indicating an extremely low-level airspace
The ceiling is 4,000 ft MSL and the floor is 1,200 ft MSL, defining the altitude band of the outer ring
The ceiling is 4,000 ft MSL above airport elevation and the floor is 1,200 ft MSL above airport elevation, defining the outer shelf
The numbers represent the ceiling and floor in hundreds of feet MSL: ceiling at 4,000 ft MSL, floor at 1,200 ft MSL

explanations.a: 40 and 12 on a sectional chart represent hundreds of feet MSL, not literal feet AGL; 40 = 4,000 ft MSL and 12 = 1,200 ft MSL.
explanations.b: This answer states essentially the same thing as the correct answer but frames it imprecisely; the notation is in hundreds of feet MSL: 40 = 4,000 ft MSL, 12 = 1,200 ft MSL.
explanations.c: The altitudes in sectional chart Class C notation are MSL values in hundreds of feet; while phrased similarly, this answer introduces unnecessary ambiguity with 'above airport elevation.'
explanations.d: On sectional charts, Class C airspace ceiling and floor values are expressed in hundreds of feet MSL; 40/12 means the ceiling is 4,000 ft MSL and the floor is 1,200 ft MSL, defining the outer shelf boundaries.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.4 Class D airspace surface area and operating hours
questions.keyword: Class D surface area extends 4.4 nm radius
questions.text: A remote pilot plans to fly within the airspace of a regional airport that has a part-time control tower and no approach control. The airport is designated Class D during tower operating hours. What is the approximate typical lateral radius of Class D airspace from the primary airport?

answers.text: Approximately 4.4 nautical miles, though the actual boundary may vary and is depicted on sectional charts
Approximately 20 nautical miles, which is the same Mode C veil radius used at large hub airports
Approximately 10 nautical miles, matching the outer ring of Class C airspace at comparable airports
Approximately 1 nautical mile, sized to contain only the immediate runway environment and traffic pattern

explanations.a: Class D airspace typically extends approximately 4.4 nautical miles from the primary airport, though the exact shape and size can vary and is depicted by the blue segmented circle on sectional charts.
explanations.b: 20 nautical miles is the Mode C veil radius for Class B airspace, not Class D; Class D is a much smaller surface area.
explanations.c: 10 nautical miles is the approximate outer ring of Class C airspace, not Class D; Class D is considerably smaller.
explanations.d: 1 nautical mile is far too small for Class D; it would not adequately contain standard traffic pattern operations at most airports.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.4 Class D airspace surface area and operating hours
questions.keyword: Class D tower closure airspace reversion Class E G
questions.text: A remote pilot plans to fly at 300 ft AGL within the normal Class D footprint of a regional airport. The airport tower is scheduled to close at 9:00 PM. The remote pilot begins the flight at 9:30 PM — after tower closure. No NOTAM has modified the airspace. What airspace classification governs this operation?

answers.text: The airspace reverts to Class E or Class G as charted when the tower closes, and ATC authorization is no longer required for the sUAS flight
The airspace remains Class D for 30 minutes after official tower closure as a buffer period to protect departing traffic
The airspace automatically becomes Class B when the tower closes because the airport's instrument approaches remain active
The airspace becomes uncontrolled Class G regardless of any charted transition area since all controlled airspace requires an active tower

explanations.a: When a part-time Class D tower closes, the airspace reverts to the airspace charted for the after-hours period, which is typically Class E (if a transition area exists) or Class G; ATC authorization is not required for sUAS operations in Class G or non-surface Class E.
explanations.b: There is no 30-minute buffer period; the airspace reverts immediately to what is charted for after-hours operations when the tower closes.
explanations.c: Tower closure does not cause reversion to Class B; Class B is a permanent designation at major hub airports and not related to tower operational hours at regional airports.
explanations.d: Charted transition areas may establish Class E airspace that persists after tower closure; the airspace does not automatically become Class G at all towers when they close.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.5 Class E airspace types and floors
questions.keyword: Class E surface area magenta dashed line
questions.text: A remote pilot studies a sectional chart and sees a magenta dashed line surrounding a small public-use airport that does not have an air traffic control tower. This symbol indicates the airport has a specific type of Class E airspace. What does the magenta dashed circle represent?

answers.text: A Mode C veil requiring all aircraft to be equipped with altitude-encoding transponders within this ring
A Class D surface area that is active only when the tower is in operation during published hours
A Class C outer ring indicating radar approach control services are available at this non-towered airport
A Class E surface area where Class E airspace begins at the surface to accommodate instrument approaches at non-towered airports

explanations.a: The Mode C veil is depicted differently on charts and is associated with Class B airports; it is not what the magenta dashed circle represents.
explanations.b: A magenta dashed line does not depict Class D airspace; Class D is shown with a blue segmented circle and applies only to towered airports.
explanations.c: Class C airspace is depicted with solid magenta rings, not dashed lines; the dashed magenta circle specifically identifies Class E surface areas.
explanations.d: A magenta dashed line on a sectional chart indicates a Class E surface area, where Class E airspace extends from the surface up; this designation is used at airports with instrument approaches but no control tower, requiring instrument weather separation at the surface.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.5 Class E airspace types and floors
questions.keyword: Class E floor 700 ft AGL magenta vignette
questions.text: A remote pilot sees a magenta shaded vignette (fade) on a sectional chart around an airport. This shading transitions from a solid magenta color near the airport outward to the background color. What does this symbol indicate about the airspace in that area?

answers.text: It indicates a Class B airspace boundary where radar services transition from mandatory to advisory beyond the shaded ring
It depicts a prohibited area where all civil aircraft including sUAS are excluded without prior FAA authorization
It marks a Military Operations Area (MOA) boundary where military training activities may be conducted at low altitudes
It indicates that Class E airspace begins at 700 ft AGL in the shaded area, transitioning instrument traffic from Class G at lower altitudes

explanations.a: Magenta vignette shading is not a Class B boundary indicator; Class B is shown with solid blue lines in segmented circles.
explanations.b: Prohibited areas are shown with blue hatch lines labeled with a 'P' prefix, not as a magenta vignette.
explanations.c: MOA boundaries are depicted with magenta hatch lines or outlined areas with specific notation, not as a vignette fade.
explanations.d: A magenta vignette or fade on a sectional chart indicates that Class E airspace begins at 700 ft AGL in that area, providing a transition area where IFR traffic transitions between the en route environment and the airport environment; below 700 ft AGL in that area the airspace is Class G.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.5 Class E airspace types and floors
questions.keyword: Class E to surface controlled airspace sUAS authorization
questions.text: A remote pilot intends to fly at 200 ft AGL within a magenta-dashed Class E surface area around a non-towered instrument airport. No waiver is held. Under 14 CFR Part 107, does this operation require ATC authorization?

answers.text: Yes, because a Class E surface area is controlled airspace beginning at the surface, and 107.41 requires authorization for operations in surface Class E
No, because 200 ft AGL is below the Class E floor of 700 ft AGL at all instrument airports
No, because the airport is non-towered and Class E is uncontrolled airspace that requires no authorization for sUAS
Yes, but only if the sUAS will be operating within the final approach course of an active instrument approach procedure

explanations.a: Under 14 CFR 107.41, sUAS operations in Class B, C, D, and surface Class E airspace require ATC authorization; a magenta-dashed Class E surface area is controlled airspace from the surface and is subject to this requirement.
explanations.b: A Class E surface area, depicted by the magenta dashed line, begins at the surface — not at 700 ft AGL; 200 ft AGL is within this surface-based Class E and requires authorization.
explanations.c: Class E is controlled airspace; while it does not have an operating control tower, it is not uncontrolled airspace, and the surface Class E designation requires ATC authorization for sUAS under Part 107.
explanations.d: The authorization requirement applies throughout the Class E surface area, not only within instrument approach corridors; the entire surface area designation triggers the authorization requirement.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: Class G uncontrolled airspace sUAS no ATC authorization needed
questions.text: A remote pilot operates in a rural area far from any airport. After checking the sectional chart, the pilot confirms the airspace at the intended altitude is Class G. Under 14 CFR Part 107, what ATC authorization is required to operate in Class G airspace?

answers.text: No ATC authorization is required; Class G is uncontrolled airspace and Part 107 does not require authorization for sUAS operations there
ATC authorization through LAANC must be obtained at least one hour before operating in any airspace including Class G
The remote pilot must file a NOTAM through FAA Flight Service describing the operation before any sUAS flight in Class G
Written authorization from the nearest FSDO must be on file before operating in any outdoor airspace under Part 107

explanations.a: Class G airspace is uncontrolled airspace; under 14 CFR 107.41, ATC authorization is required only in Class B, C, D, and surface-based Class E airspace — not in Class G.
explanations.b: LAANC authorization is required only for controlled airspace classes (B, C, D, and surface Class E); Class G requires no ATC authorization.
explanations.c: Filing a NOTAM is not a regulatory requirement for routine Part 107 operations in Class G airspace; no pre-flight notification to ATC is mandated.
explanations.d: FSDO written authorization is not required for standard Part 107 sUAS operations in any airspace class; this is not a regulatory requirement in Part 107.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: Class G ceiling below Class E en route 1200 AGL
questions.text: A remote pilot is planning a flight in an area not depicted with any special airspace markings and located more than 20 miles from any airport. According to FAA airspace classification, Class G airspace in this area typically extends from the surface to what altitude?

answers.text: Class G extends from the surface to 1,200 ft AGL, where Class E en route airspace begins in most areas
Class G extends from the surface to 14,500 ft MSL in all U.S. airspace that is not specifically designated as another class
Class G extends from the surface to 18,000 ft MSL in all rural areas more than 5 miles from any public-use airport
Class G extends from the surface to 700 ft AGL, above which Class E transition airspace begins in all U.S. domestic airspace

explanations.a: In most areas of the contiguous U.S., Class G airspace extends from the surface to 1,200 ft AGL (or to 700 ft AGL near transition areas), where Class E en route or transition airspace begins; in remote areas without transition shading, 1,200 ft AGL is the typical Class G ceiling.
explanations.b: 14,500 ft MSL is the floor of Class E en route airspace in specific areas (such as the western U.S. continental shelf), not a universal Class G ceiling; in most areas Class G extends only to 1,200 ft AGL.
explanations.c: 18,000 ft MSL is the floor of Class A airspace; Class G does not extend to 18,000 ft MSL in any standard domestic airspace scenario.
explanations.d: 700 ft AGL is the Class G ceiling in areas depicted with the magenta transition area shading; outside those transition zones, Class G extends to 1,200 ft AGL in most standard en route areas.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.7 Restricted areas prohibition and entry rules
questions.keyword: Restricted area sUAS prohibited without authorization
questions.text: A remote pilot identifies a Restricted area on the sectional chart overlapping the intended flight path. The restricted area is active during the scheduled flight time. Under 14 CFR Part 71 and Part 107, what must the remote PIC do before entering this Restricted area?

answers.text: Obtain permission from the controlling agency designated for that Restricted area before entering when the area is active
Enter the Restricted area if the flight will remain below 400 ft AGL, because sUAS are exempt from Restricted area entry requirements
File a NOTAM listing the entry time and notify the FAA Flight Service Station of the intended overflight
Proceed through the Restricted area using LAANC authorization if it is active and the sUAS remains in Class G airspace

explanations.a: Entry into an active Restricted area requires permission from the controlling agency listed for that area on the sectional chart or in the FAA Chart Supplement; LAANC and DroneZone do not provide Restricted area authorization.
explanations.b: sUAS are not exempt from Restricted area entry requirements; Part 107 applies to all airspace rules including special use airspace.
explanations.c: Filing a NOTAM does not grant permission to enter a Restricted area; authorization must come from the designated controlling agency.
explanations.d: LAANC addresses ATC authorization in controlled airspace classes but does not authorize entry into special use airspace such as Restricted areas.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: Prohibited area entry categorically forbidden
questions.text: A remote pilot's proposed flight path crosses P-56, a Prohibited area over the Washington D.C. area. The pilot has LAANC authorization for Class B airspace in the area. Under FAA regulations, may the remote pilot enter P-56 with this authorization?

answers.text: Yes, provided the sUAS remains below 400 ft AGL and does not fly over any federal buildings within the Prohibited area boundary
Yes, LAANC authorization for Class B airspace implicitly covers all subordinate airspace designations within that Class B boundary
No, Prohibited areas require a separate FAA waiver distinct from LAANC, but such waivers are available through the standard DroneZone portal
No, Prohibited areas may not be entered by any civil aircraft including sUAS under any circumstance without specific presidential or DOD authorization

explanations.a: Altitude limits and building avoidance do not create an exception to the Prohibited area prohibition; all civil aircraft are barred from entry without proper authorization.
explanations.b: LAANC authorization addresses ATC separation requirements for controlled airspace; it does not override Prohibited area restrictions that apply to all civil aircraft.
explanations.c: A standard DroneZone waiver does not provide authorization to enter Prohibited areas; authorization for entry into Prohibited areas is not available through the standard Part 107 waiver system.
explanations.d: Prohibited areas established under 14 CFR Part 71 represent areas where flight is prohibited for national security or other compelling reasons; civil aircraft, including sUAS, may not enter without specific authorization from the controlling authority, which is far beyond standard FAA waiver processes.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: MOA non-participating civil aircraft caution advisory
questions.text: A remote pilot notices their planned flight path crosses an active Military Operations Area (MOA) depicted on the sectional chart. Under 14 CFR regulations and FAA guidance, what is the correct approach for a Part 107 sUAS operation in an active MOA?

answers.text: Obtain ATC authorization through LAANC before entering the MOA because it is classified as controlled airspace
File a NOTAM identifying the sUAS operation within the MOA, which automatically notifies military units of the civil aircraft presence
Contact the controlling agency, determine whether high-speed military activity is occurring, exercise extreme caution or avoid the area, and remain vigilant for military aircraft
Proceed with the flight if below 400 ft AGL because MOA restrictions apply only to aircraft operating under instrument flight rules

explanations.a: MOAs are not controlled airspace requiring ATC authorization for entry; they are special use airspace where civil aircraft may enter but must exercise extreme caution.
explanations.b: Filing a NOTAM does not automatically notify military units and is not the standard procedure for civil aircraft entering a MOA; direct contact with the controlling agency is more appropriate.
explanations.c: When a MOA is active, civil aircraft operators should contact the controlling agency (listed on the chart) or ATC for status, exercise extreme caution when inside an active MOA, and remain alert for military aircraft that may be operating at high speeds and unpredictable altitudes.
explanations.d: MOA restrictions apply to all aircraft, not only IFR aircraft; while civil VFR aircraft may legally enter an active MOA, extreme caution is required due to high-speed military activity.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.7 Warning areas offshore special use airspace
questions.keyword: Warning area international airspace no ATC authorization required
questions.text: A remote pilot operating near the Atlantic coast identifies a Warning area on the sectional chart overlapping the planned offshore flight path. Warning areas differ from Restricted areas in a key legal sense. What is the primary operational distinction between a Warning area and a Restricted area?

answers.text: Warning areas require the same prior-authorization standard as Prohibited areas and may never be entered by civil aircraft
Warning areas contain exclusively anti-aircraft artillery ranges, while Restricted areas contain only aerial gunnery ranges used by military fighters
Warning areas are located over international waters where the FAA cannot legally prohibit civil aircraft entry, but they contain hazardous military activities requiring extreme caution
Warning areas apply only to manned aircraft; Part 107 sUAS are specifically exempted from all Warning area restrictions and advisories

explanations.a: Warning areas do not carry the same entry prohibition as Restricted or Prohibited areas; their international water location means the FAA cannot legally restrict civil aircraft as it can over domestic U.S. airspace.
explanations.b: Both Warning areas and Restricted areas can encompass various military activities; the distinction is jurisdictional, not based on the type of military activity.
explanations.c: Warning areas are established over international airspace (typically offshore waters) where the FAA lacks the authority to prohibit civil aircraft entry; however, hazardous military training activities occur there and all aircraft must exercise extreme caution.
explanations.d: Part 107 sUAS are subject to the same warning advisories as manned aircraft operating in Warning areas; there is no exemption for sUAS in FAA Advisory Circulars or Part 107 regarding Warning areas.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: sectional chart airport blue vs magenta color manned vs towered
questions.text: A remote pilot is learning to interpret sectional aeronautical charts and notices that some airports are depicted in blue while others are in magenta. What does this color difference signify about the airports?

answers.text: Blue airports have paved runways while magenta airports have unpaved or grass runways, indicating different surface conditions
Blue airports are military airports while magenta airports are civil public-use airports open to general aviation
Blue airports have instrument approach procedures while magenta airports are VFR-only airports without instrument approaches
Blue airports have an operating control tower while magenta airports are non-towered airports

explanations.a: Runway surface type is not indicated by airport symbol color on sectional charts; the color codes indicate tower status.
explanations.b: Military airports are depicted with specific military symbols; the blue versus magenta distinction applies to tower status, not military vs. civil ownership.
explanations.c: Instrument approach procedures are not indicated by airport color on sectionals; separate IFR approach plates and the magenta dashed surface area circle indicate instrument approaches at non-towered airports.
explanations.d: On FAA sectional aeronautical charts, airports depicted in blue have an operating control tower (ATC), while airports depicted in magenta are non-towered airports; this color distinction directly affects whether a remote pilot needs ATC authorization to operate in the associated airspace.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: sectional chart MSL elevation number airport
questions.text: A remote pilot reads a sectional chart and notices a number next to an airport symbol that reads '1243'. When planning an sUAS flight that will maintain 400 ft AGL above this airport, what does the 1243 figure represent and why does it matter?

answers.text: 1243 indicates the airport field elevation in feet MSL; combined with 400 ft AGL, the sUAS would be at approximately 1,643 ft MSL
1243 indicates the airport's traffic pattern altitude in feet AGL; the remote pilot must remain 400 ft below 1243 ft AGL during all operations
1243 represents the number of instrument approaches available at the airport; higher numbers indicate more complex airspace
1243 indicates the highest obstacle within 5 nautical miles of the airport in feet MSL, defining the minimum safe sUAS altitude

explanations.a: The number next to an airport symbol on a sectional chart represents the airport field elevation in feet above mean sea level (MSL); for an sUAS operating at 400 ft AGL, the MSL altitude would be approximately 1,643 ft MSL (1,243 + 400).
explanations.b: Traffic pattern altitude is not depicted as a plain number next to the airport symbol; the number alongside an airport symbol on a sectional represents field elevation MSL.
explanations.c: The number of instrument approaches is not depicted as a standalone number alongside the airport symbol; this information is found in the Chart Supplement.
explanations.d: Obstacle heights are depicted with separate obstacle symbols; the plain number next to the airport symbol is always the field elevation MSL.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: obstacle symbol high obstruction 1000 ft AGL and above
questions.text: While reviewing a sectional chart for preflight planning, a remote pilot observes a bold-outlined obstacle symbol with the numbers '1549' above the symbol and '(421)' below it in parentheses. What information do these two numbers convey about the obstacle?

answers.text: 1549 is the obstacle latitude coordinate and 421 is the obstacle longitude coordinate on the sectional chart grid
1549 is the FAA obstacle identification number and (421) is the number of aircraft that must avoid this obstacle under Part 91
1549 is the obstacle height in feet MSL and (421) is the obstacle height in feet AGL above the surrounding terrain
1549 is the obstacle height in feet AGL and (421) is the obstacle height in feet MSL; bold symbology means the obstacle is a radio tower

explanations.a: Coordinates are not displayed in this format next to obstacle symbols; the numbers represent the obstacle's height in two reference systems.
explanations.b: FAA obstacle identification numbers and manned aviation avoidance requirements are not depicted in this format on sectional charts.
explanations.c: On FAA sectional charts, the number above (or beside) an obstacle symbol represents the obstacle's elevation above mean sea level (MSL), and the number in parentheses represents the obstacle's height above ground level (AGL); 1549 ft MSL and 421 ft AGL in this example.
explanations.d: The MSL and AGL values are always in that order — MSL on top, AGL in parentheses below — not reversed; the bold outline indicates the obstacle exceeds 1,000 ft AGL, which is a key threshold for remote pilots.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: Military Training Route MTR IR VR chart depiction
questions.text: A sectional chart shows several lines labeled 'IR177' and 'VR1207' crossing the remote pilot's planned operating area. The remote pilot is unfamiliar with these designations. What do IR and VR routes represent, and how should a remote pilot consider them during preflight planning?

answers.text: IR and VR are Instrument Routes and VFR Routes used by general aviation aircraft under flight following that require TCAS awareness
IR and VR are International Routes and Visual Routes, depicting commercial airline jet routes that all sUAS must avoid by at least 5 miles
IR and VR are Military Training Routes flown at high speed and low altitude by military aircraft; remote pilots should be aware of potential high-speed military traffic along these routes
IR and VR routes depict IFR and VFR airways that are exclusive to manned aircraft and automatically prohibited to all sUAS regardless of altitude

explanations.a: IR (IFR Military Training Routes) and VR (VFR Military Training Routes) are military-specific designations, not general aviation flight following routes.
explanations.b: IR and VR are not international or commercial routes; they are Military Training Routes flown by military aircraft at low altitudes and high speeds.
explanations.c: Military Training Routes (MTRs) designated IR (flown under IFR) and VR (flown under VFR) are used by military aircraft for high-speed, low-altitude flight training; remote pilots should check for active MTRs during preflight because military aircraft may be operating at very high speeds and low altitudes along these routes, posing a significant see-and-avoid hazard.
explanations.d: MTRs are not categorically prohibited to civil aircraft or sUAS; they are advisory overlays indicating potential military activity, not exclusive restricted airspace.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: stadium TFR 3 nm radius game day prohibition
questions.text: A remote pilot wants to fly an sUAS near a professional football stadium during a scheduled home game. A game-day Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR) has been issued under 14 CFR 91.145. What is the standard protected airspace radius of a stadium TFR during a major sporting event?

answers.text: 1 nautical mile radius, from the surface to 3,000 ft AGL, active from 1 hour before kickoff to 1 hour after the game ends
10 nautical miles radius, from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL, applied only to large NFL and MLB venues with more than 30,000 seats
5 nautical miles radius, from 500 ft AGL to 18,000 ft MSL, active during all home games for the entire sport season
3 nautical miles radius from the stadium, from the surface to 3,000 ft AGL, active from 1 hour before the event to 1 hour after

explanations.a: The stadium TFR radius is 3 nm, not 1 nm; the 1 nm figure is too small to protect the airspace around a large sports venue.
explanations.b: 10 nautical miles and 10,000 ft MSL are associated with VIP TFRs and major security events, not standard stadium TFRs; the stadium TFR standard is 3 nm to 3,000 ft AGL.
explanations.c: 5 nautical miles and 18,000 ft MSL describe a different, larger TFR category; the standard stadium TFR is 3 nm radius to 3,000 ft AGL.
explanations.d: Under 14 CFR 91.145, a TFR around a major sporting event such as an NFL game establishes a 3-nautical-mile radius from the stadium, from the surface to 3,000 ft AGL, effective 1 hour before the event and ending 1 hour after the event concludes.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: presidential TFR 30 nm 10 nm inner ring
questions.text: A TFR has been issued for a presidential visit to a city. The remote pilot is trying to understand the dimensions of a standard presidential TFR. Under 14 CFR 91.141, what airspace protections does a presidential TFR typically establish?

answers.text: A single 5-nautical-mile radius prohibition zone from the surface to 18,000 ft MSL around the president's immediate location
A 3-nautical-mile security radius from the surface to 3,000 ft AGL similar in structure to a standard stadium TFR
A 10-nautical-mile inner ring prohibited to all aircraft and a 30-nautical-mile outer ring requiring ATC coordination for VFR flight
A 50-nautical-mile ADIZ-style ring requiring all aircraft to file IFR flight plans and maintain radio contact with NORAD at all times

explanations.a: The 5-mile prohibition zone does not describe the standard structure of a presidential TFR; the standard has both an inner prohibited ring and an outer coordination ring.
explanations.b: The 3 nm/3,000 ft AGL structure describes a stadium TFR under 91.145, not a presidential TFR.
explanations.c: A presidential TFR under 91.141 typically includes a 10-nautical-mile inner ring where all aircraft are prohibited except those with specific authorization, and a 30-nautical-mile outer ring where VFR flight requires specific coordination; both areas prohibit standard sUAS operations.
explanations.d: A 50-nm ADIZ-style ring is not the structure of a standard presidential TFR; the inner/outer ring structure described in answer B is the correct framework.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: disaster TFR 91.137 wildfire national emergency
questions.text: Wildfire crews are battling an active forest fire. The FAA has issued a Temporary Flight Restriction over the fire area under 14 CFR 91.137. A remote pilot is contacted by a news organization to fly over the fire and broadcast live footage. Which statement accurately describes the remote pilot's authorization status under this TFR?

answers.text: The remote pilot may fly immediately because news media have an unconditional right under the First Amendment to access airspace over natural disasters
The remote pilot may fly freely below 200 ft AGL because disaster TFRs apply only to aircraft operating above 1,000 ft AGL
The remote pilot must obtain authorization from the agency controlling the TFR; media access may be permitted but is not automatic
The remote pilot may fly after submitting a NOTAM to FAA Flight Service indicating the media purpose of the flight

explanations.a: First Amendment protections for newsgathering do not override FAA airspace restrictions; media organizations must still obtain authorization from the controlling agency to operate within a disaster TFR.
explanations.b: Disaster TFRs do not contain altitude floors that exempt flights below 200 ft AGL; the TFR applies throughout the designated altitude block regardless of how low the aircraft operates.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 91.137, disaster TFRs restrict airspace to protect emergency response operations; news media aircraft may receive authorization from the controlling agency but must affirmatively request and receive that authorization before entering the TFR.
explanations.d: Filing a NOTAM does not grant authorization to enter a TFR; authorization must come from the designated controlling agency.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: LAANC near-real-time authorization controlled airspace
questions.text: A remote pilot needs to fly within Class D airspace and wants to obtain authorization as quickly as possible. A colleague suggests using the Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability (LAANC). What is LAANC and how does it work for Part 107 pilots?

answers.text: LAANC is a system that provides near-real-time airspace authorization for sUAS operations in controlled airspace through FAA-approved apps and USS providers
LAANC is an FAA-run radio frequency broadcast system that remote pilots monitor to receive ATC clearances during flight in controlled airspace
LAANC is an FAA portal where remote pilots apply for waivers to operate beyond standard Part 107 limits in any airspace class
LAANC is an automated NOTAM filing system that notifies ATC facilities of sUAS operations in their terminal airspace before each flight

explanations.a: LAANC is an FAA collaboration with industry UAS Service Suppliers (USS) that provides near-real-time airspace authorization for sUAS operations in controlled airspace, allowing remote pilots to receive authorization through approved apps within seconds in many cases.
explanations.b: LAANC is not a radio frequency system; it operates through digital applications and software platforms approved by the FAA.
explanations.c: LAANC provides airspace authorization, not waivers; waivers for deviations from Part 107 operating rules are requested through the FAA DroneZone portal separately.
explanations.d: LAANC is an authorization system, not a NOTAM filing service; it grants access to controlled airspace and is not a notification-only mechanism.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: LAANC UAS facility map altitude grid ceiling
questions.text: A remote pilot uses LAANC to request authorization in Class C airspace at 300 ft AGL near an airport. The LAANC app indicates the UAS Facility Map (UASFM) shows a 200 ft ceiling for that grid square. What will the LAANC system do with the pilot's 300 ft authorization request?

answers.text: Grant the request automatically because Part 107's 400 ft AGL limit supersedes the UAS Facility Map ceiling in Class C airspace
Refer the request to the controlling ATC facility for manual review, which typically takes 3 to 5 business days
Deny the request automatically because the requested altitude exceeds the UAS Facility Map ceiling for that grid square
Approve the request at 200 ft AGL automatically, adjusting the authorization to the maximum ceiling without requiring a new request

explanations.a: The UAS Facility Map ceiling is the maximum altitude LAANC can automatically authorize; Part 107's 400 ft AGL maximum does not override the UASFM-defined ceiling for a specific grid square.
explanations.b: Requests exceeding the UASFM ceiling are not automatically sent to ATC for manual review through LAANC; they are declined by the LAANC system, and the pilot must apply through FAA DroneZone for a manual review if a higher altitude is needed.
explanations.c: LAANC can only automatically authorize altitudes up to the UAS Facility Map ceiling for each grid square; a 300 ft request in a 200 ft ceiling grid will be denied, and the pilot must pursue FAA DroneZone for manual authorization above the UASFM ceiling.
explanations.d: LAANC does not automatically adjust authorizations to the maximum UASFM ceiling when a higher request is denied; the pilot receives a denial and must submit a new request at or below the ceiling.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: DroneZone manual authorization above UASFM ceiling
questions.text: A professional aerial inspector needs to fly at 380 ft AGL in a Class D surface area grid where the LAANC UAS Facility Map shows a maximum ceiling of 100 ft. LAANC denies the request. What is the appropriate next step to legally obtain authorization at 380 ft AGL?

answers.text: The inspector may proceed at 380 ft AGL because LAANC denial is advisory only and Part 107 permits operations up to 400 ft AGL in all airspace
Refile the LAANC request in an adjacent grid square that may have a higher ceiling, then fly diagonally into the needed area
Submit a manual airspace authorization request through the FAA DroneZone portal, which allows requests above the UASFM ceiling for consideration by ATC
Contact the airport's ATIS service by radio and request verbal ATC authorization for the higher altitude before departing

explanations.a: A LAANC denial is not advisory; it means the automatic authorization pathway is unavailable and the pilot must seek another authorization method before operating.
explanations.b: Using an adjacent grid square with a higher ceiling and flying diagonally into the needed area circumvents the authorization requirements for the actual operating area and is not a compliant approach.
explanations.c: The FAA DroneZone portal allows remote pilots to submit manual airspace authorization requests, which are reviewed by ATC facilities and can approve altitudes above the UASFM ceiling when safety permits; this is the correct escalation pathway after a LAANC denial.
explanations.d: ATIS is a one-way broadcast service that cannot grant airspace authorization; ATC authorization must come through the formal LAANC or DroneZone processes, not via radio contact with ATIS.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: Class E en route floor 1200 AGL outside transition areas
questions.text: A remote pilot plans to fly at 800 ft AGL in a rural area that is not within any transition area (no magenta shading or dashed circle) and is not within 20 nm of a Class B airport. The only airspace marking in the area is the standard Class E en route airspace. What airspace class is the remote pilot operating in at 800 ft AGL?

answers.text: Class E, because Class E airspace begins at the surface throughout the entire contiguous United States regardless of chart depictions
Class G, because all airspace below 1,200 ft AGL is Class G in areas without specific transition area designations
Class G below 1,200 ft AGL where no transition area exists, meaning 800 ft AGL is still in Class G in this un-shaded rural area
Class D, because all airspace within 5 miles of any public-use airport regardless of tower status extends to 2,500 ft AGL

explanations.a: Class E does not begin at the surface throughout the entire U.S.; it begins at 1,200 ft AGL in standard en route areas, 700 ft AGL in transition areas, and at the surface only where specifically designated.
explanations.b: This answer and C say essentially the same thing; Class G does extend to 1,200 ft AGL in un-shaded rural areas, making 800 ft AGL Class G where no transition area is charted.
explanations.c: In areas not depicted with transition area shading (magenta vignette) or Class E surface designations, Class G airspace extends from the surface to 1,200 ft AGL; at 800 ft AGL the remote pilot is in Class G, which requires no ATC authorization.
explanations.d: Class D airspace is established only at airports with operating control towers and is depicted on charts; a blanket 5-mile 2,500 ft AGL rule does not exist in U.S. airspace classification.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: Class B floor above airport 10000 ft MSL ceiling
questions.text: A remote pilot studying for the Part 107 knowledge test reads a Class B airspace depiction on a sectional chart with the notation 100/SFC at the innermost ring. What does this notation communicate about the inner Class B ring?

answers.text: The ceiling is 100 ft MSL and the floor is at the surface, designating an extremely shallow Class B airspace
The notation means the ceiling is 1,000 ft AGL and 'SFC' denotes a surface frequency control requirement
The ceiling is 10,000 ft MSL and the floor extends from the surface, indicating Class B airspace that reaches from the ground to 10,000 ft MSL
The ceiling is 100 ft AGL and 'SFC' indicates the airspace is maintained by the Surface Movement Control frequency at the airport

explanations.a: On sectional charts, Class B airspace ceiling values are expressed in hundreds of feet MSL; '100' means 10,000 ft MSL, not 100 ft MSL.
explanations.b: '100' in Class B notation represents hundreds of feet MSL (10,000 ft MSL), not 1,000 ft AGL; 'SFC' means surface, not a frequency control requirement.
explanations.c: On FAA sectional charts, Class B airspace altitudes are expressed in hundreds of feet MSL; '100' represents 10,000 ft MSL and 'SFC' indicates the floor begins at the surface, meaning this innermost ring of Class B extends from ground level to 10,000 ft MSL.
explanations.d: 'SFC' in airspace notation always means the airspace floor is at the surface; 100 represents the ceiling in hundreds of feet MSL, equaling 10,000 ft MSL.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.7 Alert areas and other special use airspace
questions.keyword: Alert area civil aviation high activity caution
questions.text: A remote pilot identifies an Alert area on the sectional chart overlapping the planned flight area. Unlike Restricted areas, Alert areas have no entry restrictions for civil aircraft. What is the purpose of an Alert area, and what should a remote pilot do when planning to fly through one?

answers.text: Alert areas indicate airspace reserved exclusively for IFR training where VFR aircraft are legally prohibited without a clearance
Alert areas are temporary designations that expire after 24 hours and require no special consideration from sUAS operators
Alert areas are equivalent to Prohibited areas over critical infrastructure; entry is prohibited without written FAA authorization
Alert areas warn of a high volume of pilot training or other unusual aerial activity; civil aircraft may enter but must exercise extreme caution

explanations.a: Alert areas do not prohibit VFR aircraft; they are advisory areas indicating heightened activity that requires caution, not restricted areas.
explanations.b: Alert areas are established through the NOTAM and sectional chart system and are not necessarily temporary 24-hour designations; they are permanent or semi-permanent features on aeronautical charts requiring ongoing pilot awareness.
explanations.c: Alert areas carry no entry prohibition; they are informational advisory areas, unlike Prohibited and Restricted areas which have entry restrictions.
explanations.d: Alert areas are established to alert pilots to areas where unusual volumes of aerial training activity or other flight operations occur; all aircraft, including sUAS, may enter but must be vigilant for traffic and exercise extreme caution.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.12 Controlled vs uncontrolled airspace sUAS authorization
questions.keyword: sUAS Class C authorization same as Class B D requirement
questions.text: A remote pilot verifies the airspace at the proposed flight location is Class C based on magenta solid rings on the sectional chart. The Class C airspace is active and the airport's approach control is staffed. Under Part 107, must the remote pilot obtain ATC authorization, and if so, through what process?

answers.text: No authorization needed in Class C because sUAS below 400 ft AGL are exempt from Class C requirements that apply to manned aircraft
Yes, ATC authorization is required; LAANC or FAA DroneZone are the authorized channels for obtaining Class C airspace authorization for sUAS
Yes, but only if the sUAS will fly within the 5 nm inner ring; the outer ring of Class C does not require sUAS authorization
Yes, but the pilot must contact the approach control directly by radio to obtain a verbal clearance before launching the sUAS

explanations.a: Part 107 sUAS are not exempt from Class C airspace authorization requirements; 107.41 requires authorization for all operations in Class B, C, D, and surface Class E.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.41, sUAS operations in Class C airspace require ATC authorization; LAANC and the FAA DroneZone portal are the designated methods for obtaining this authorization.
explanations.c: The authorization requirement applies throughout the entire Class C airspace, both the inner and outer rings; there is no outer-ring exemption for sUAS.
explanations.d: Radio contact with approach control is the manned aviation method; sUAS remote pilots use LAANC or DroneZone, not direct radio communication with ATC, to obtain Class C authorization.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.12 Controlled vs uncontrolled airspace sUAS authorization
questions.keyword: non-surface Class E 1200 AGL no sUAS authorization
questions.text: A remote pilot's planned flight path at 350 ft AGL passes through an area depicted with the standard Class E en route shading beginning at 1,200 ft AGL. No transition area or surface-based Class E is charted. Under Part 107, does this flight require ATC authorization for the non-surface Class E airspace?

answers.text: No, because the flight at 350 ft AGL is entirely within Class G airspace below the 1,200 ft AGL Class E floor
Yes, but only NOTAM filing is required rather than formal LAANC or DroneZone authorization
Yes, all Class E airspace regardless of floor altitude requires ATC authorization under 14 CFR 107.41
No, but the remote pilot must carry a current sectional chart as evidence of the Class G operating environment

explanations.a: If Class E begins at 1,200 ft AGL and the flight is at 350 ft AGL, the aircraft is operating in Class G airspace (which exists below the Class E floor); no ATC authorization is needed for Class G operations under Part 107.
explanations.b: NOTAM filing is not a Part 107 authorization mechanism; the key point is that flying below the Class E floor at 350 ft AGL puts the sUAS in Class G, which requires no authorization.
explanations.c: 14 CFR 107.41 requires ATC authorization only for Class B, C, D, and surface-based Class E airspace; non-surface Class E airspace (such as en route Class E beginning at 1,200 ft AGL) does not require authorization.
explanations.d: Carrying a sectional chart is good practice but is not a regulatory requirement to operate in Class G; no authorization document is required for Class G sUAS operations.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: VOR symbol sectional chart navigation aid
questions.text: While reviewing a sectional chart, a remote pilot notices a compass rose centered on a small hexagonal symbol with the label 'RICHMOND VOR 115.4 RIC.' Why is awareness of VOR locations relevant to a remote pilot during preflight planning?

answers.text: VOR stations emit signals that interfere with sUAS compass systems within a 5-mile radius, requiring the pilot to disable autopilot near VORs
VOR airways (Victor airways) are depicted between VOR stations; understanding their locations helps the remote pilot identify areas of en route IFR and VFR traffic
Remote pilots must file their intended route relative to the nearest VOR when operating above 200 ft AGL in Class G airspace
VOR locations mark the exact center of each state's Class B airspace boundary and must be avoided by all Part 107 sUAS without exception

explanations.a: VOR signals do not interfere with sUAS compass or autopilot systems in any significant way recognized by FAA guidance; this statement is factually incorrect.
explanations.b: VOR stations serve as the anchor points for Victor airways (V airways), which are IFR and VFR airways used by manned aircraft; understanding VOR locations helps the remote pilot identify likely areas of manned aircraft traffic, improving see-and-avoid planning.
explanations.c: There is no route-filing requirement relative to VORs for sUAS operations in Class G; this is not a Part 107 requirement.
explanations.d: VOR stations are not related to Class B airspace boundaries; Class B airspace is defined independently of VOR placement.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: sectional chart contour lines terrain elevation reading
questions.text: A remote pilot is planning an operation over hilly terrain using a sectional chart. Brown contour lines are visible across the planned flight area, with the numbers 800 and 1000 appearing on adjacent contour lines. Why is understanding contour line values important for this sUAS operation?

answers.text: Contour lines at 800 and 1000 indicate the MSL altitude bands where Class E and Class G airspace boundaries are located in mountainous terrain
Contour lines show the altitude of the traffic pattern at nearby airports, which varies with terrain elevation in mountainous areas
Contour lines indicate restricted zones where terrain-following flight is prohibited for all unmanned aircraft under Part 107 Section 107.19
Contour lines depict terrain elevation in feet MSL; understanding terrain elevation helps the remote pilot maintain the 400 ft AGL ceiling above the actual ground surface rather than above sea level

explanations.a: Contour lines on sectional charts depict terrain elevation, not airspace class boundaries; airspace boundaries are depicted with separate lines and symbols.
explanations.b: Traffic pattern altitudes are not shown as contour lines; they are separate values found in the Chart Supplement and on airport diagrams.
explanations.c: Contour lines do not designate restricted zones; they are topographic elevation lines with no regulatory restriction attached to them.
explanations.d: Brown contour lines on sectional charts represent terrain elevation in feet MSL; a remote pilot must understand local terrain elevation to correctly calculate the 400 ft AGL ceiling over varying terrain — at 1,000 ft MSL terrain, the AGL ceiling equates to approximately 1,400 ft MSL, for example.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: sectional maximum elevation figure MEF quadrant
questions.text: A remote pilot notices large blue numbers reading '47' in the center of a sectional chart quadrant. This figure appears to be the Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF) for that quadrant. What does the MEF of 47 indicate, and how should the remote pilot apply it during planning?

answers.text: The MEF of 47 means the maximum wind speed in knots recorded in that quadrant over the past 12 months; values above 25 require sUAS operational restrictions
The MEF of 47 indicates the highest known obstacle or terrain in that quadrant reaches 4,700 ft MSL; the remote pilot should ensure sUAS operations account for this when planning altitude clearance
The MEF of 47 represents the quadrant's average ground elevation of 4,700 ft MSL, below which sUAS operations are prohibited without a waiver
The MEF of 47 means the quadrant contains 47 charted obstacles and the pilot must identify each one before flight

explanations.a: MEF values represent elevation, not wind speed; the Maximum Elevation Figure relates to the highest terrain or obstacle in the quadrant.
explanations.b: The Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF) is expressed in hundreds of feet MSL; an MEF of 47 means the highest known obstacle or terrain in that latitude-longitude quadrant reaches 4,700 ft MSL, including a buffer above the highest charted feature; this helps remote pilots understand the maximum terrain/obstacle elevation in the area.
explanations.c: MEF is an elevation reference for the highest point in the quadrant, not an average ground elevation; it does not establish a floor below which operations are prohibited.
explanations.d: MEF represents a single maximum elevation value for the quadrant, not a count of obstacles; obstacle counts are not depicted on sectional charts in this format.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.12 Controlled vs uncontrolled airspace sUAS authorization
questions.keyword: non-towered airport Class G no authorization below 700 AGL
questions.text: A remote pilot plans to fly at 150 ft AGL approximately 1 mile from a small non-towered general aviation airport. The sectional chart shows no Class D, Class C, or Class E surface area around this airport. The airspace at 150 ft AGL is Class G. Under Part 107, what authorization is required for this operation?

answers.text: No ATC authorization is needed because the operation is entirely within Class G airspace
LAANC authorization is required within 5 miles of any public-use airport regardless of airspace class
A written notification to the airport manager is required at least 24 hours before any flight within 2 miles of a non-towered airport
NOTAM filing through FAA Flight Service is required to alert traffic pattern aircraft to the sUAS presence within 1 mile of the airport

explanations.a: Under current 14 CFR 107.41, ATC authorization is required only in Class B, C, D, and surface Class E airspace; Class G airspace requires no ATC authorization regardless of proximity to a non-towered airport.
explanations.b: The 5-mile airport notification requirement was part of the original Part 107 rule but was superseded; the authorization requirement is now based on airspace class, not distance from the airport.
explanations.c: Written notification to the airport manager is not a current Part 107 requirement; the old 5-mile notification rule was replaced by the airspace class-based authorization system.
explanations.d: NOTAM filing is not required for routine Part 107 operations in Class G near a non-towered airport; it remains good practice to use see-and-avoid procedures and monitor the CTAF.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: Chart Supplement airport information services ATIS AWOS
questions.text: A remote pilot wants to check weather conditions at a nearby airport before an sUAS flight. The sectional chart shows a small square symbol containing the letter 'A' next to the airport frequency information. In the context of airport services, what does this 'A' designation typically indicate?

answers.text: The airport has an active air traffic control tower that provides Class A airspace services above 18,000 ft MSL
The airport is designated as an Alternate landing airport for commercial air carrier operations during diversion events
The airport has an Automated Weather Observing System (AWOS) or Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) providing continuous weather data
The airport has an Automated Terminal Information Service (ATIS) broadcast providing weather and airport status information

explanations.a: The 'A' designation does not relate to Class A airspace; that airspace class begins at 18,000 ft MSL and is a separate concept from airport services.
explanations.b: Alternate airport designation is not indicated by an 'A' on sectional chart frequency boxes; this is an IFR flight planning concept.
explanations.c: AWOS and ASOS are depicted with different notations on charts; the ATIS frequency is specifically identified by the 'A' designation in the airport communication box.
explanations.d: On FAA sectional charts and in the Chart Supplement, the 'A' preceding a frequency in the airport communication box indicates the ATIS (Automated Terminal Information Service) frequency; ATIS provides recorded non-control weather, NOTAMs, and airport status information that remote pilots can use during preflight planning.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: NOTAM preflight check TFR obligation every flight
questions.text: Before each sUAS operation, a remote pilot is obligated to check for active and newly issued Temporary Flight Restrictions. Under 14 CFR 107.49, which resource is considered the authoritative source for checking active TFRs applicable to a planned sUAS operation?

answers.text: The remote pilot's sUAS manufacturer app, which automatically downloads all TFRs at application startup each day
The FAA Notices to Air Missions (NOTAMs) system, accessible through FAA NOTAM Search, 1800wxbrief.com, or approved aviation apps
The FAA's annual aeronautical chart update, which includes all semi-permanent TFRs that are expected to last more than 30 days
The local airport manager, who is required by FAA regulation to post all active TFRs within 20 miles on a public bulletin board

explanations.a: Manufacturer apps may display TFR data but are not the authoritative FAA source; TFR compliance requires checking official FAA NOTAM sources.
explanations.b: NOTAMs (Notices to Air Missions) are the official FAA mechanism for publishing TFRs; the FAA NOTAM Search website, 1800wxbrief.com, and FAA-approved planning tools that pull live NOTAM data are the authoritative sources for current TFR status.
explanations.c: Annual chart updates do not include TFRs, which are temporary and dynamic; TFRs can be issued minutes before a flight and require a real-time check.
explanations.d: Airport managers are not required by FAA regulation to post TFR information; the responsibility for preflight TFR checks falls entirely on the remote pilot.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.7 Restricted areas prohibition and entry rules
questions.keyword: Restricted area inactive period entry permitted
questions.text: A remote pilot wants to fly an sUAS through a designated Restricted area labeled R-2508 on the sectional chart. The remote pilot calls the controlling agency and is told the Restricted area is not active during the planned flight window. Under these conditions, may the remote pilot conduct the sUAS operation within R-2508?

answers.text: No, Restricted areas are always active regardless of the time of day and may never be entered by civil aircraft
Yes, but only if the sUAS remains below 200 ft AGL to stay clear of any residual military traffic from prior exercises
Yes, but the remote pilot must file a NOTAM confirming the controlling agency's verbal clearance before entering the Restricted area
Yes, when the controlling agency confirms the Restricted area is inactive, civil aircraft including sUAS may enter the area without restriction

explanations.a: Restricted areas are not always active; they have published hours of use and may be released to civil aviation when not in use by the controlling agency.
explanations.b: No altitude restriction applies when an Restricted area is confirmed inactive; the remote pilot may operate normally within the area once its inactive status is confirmed.
explanations.c: A NOTAM filing is not required to confirm verbal clearance from the controlling agency; direct confirmation that the area is inactive and released is sufficient.
explanations.d: When the controlling agency responsible for a Restricted area confirms it is inactive and the airspace is returned to the controlling ATC facility, civil aircraft including sUAS may operate within the area without special authorization; this is confirmed through direct contact with the controlling agency or ATC.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.2 Class B airspace structure and sUAS authorization requirement
questions.keyword: Class B Mode C veil 30 nm ring manned aircraft
questions.text: A remote pilot is planning a flight 25 nautical miles from a Class B primary airport. The Mode C veil for that Class B extends 30 nm from the airport. While the Mode C veil requires manned aircraft within 30 nm to have altitude-encoding transponders, does this veil create any additional authorization requirement for sUAS operations within 25 nm under Part 107?

answers.text: No, the Mode C transponder requirement under 91.215 applies to manned aircraft; Part 107 separately prohibits ADS-B Out and transponders on sUAS, and sUAS authorization is based on actual airspace class, not the Mode C veil
Yes, sUAS must carry an altitude-encoding transponder that complies with Mode C requirements within the 30 nm veil
Yes, sUAS must obtain ATC authorization within the Mode C veil regardless of the actual airspace class at the operating altitude
No, sUAS under 55 pounds are categorically exempt from all Mode C veil restrictions in both Part 91 and Part 107

explanations.a: The Mode C veil under 14 CFR 91.215 is a manned aircraft equipment requirement; Part 107 prohibits ADS-B Out and transponders on sUAS under 107.67, and sUAS authorization is determined by actual airspace class (B, C, D, surface E), not by proximity to Class B within the Mode C veil.
explanations.b: Part 107 prohibits transponders and ADS-B Out on sUAS; carrying Mode C equipment is not permitted and is not required by the Mode C veil for sUAS.
explanations.c: The Mode C veil does not create a separate airspace authorization requirement for sUAS; the authorization requirement under 107.41 is based on the airspace class (B, C, D, or surface E) at the operating location and altitude.
explanations.d: While sUAS are not subject to Mode C transponder requirements, this is because Part 107 prohibits such equipment entirely, not because of a blanket weight-based exemption from the veil.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: prohibited area blue hatch P- designation national security
questions.text: On a sectional chart, a remote pilot observes a blue-hatched area labeled 'P-40' near a major city. No altitude information is shown inside the hatching. What does this charted feature represent?

answers.text: P-40 is a Parachute Jump Zone where manned aircraft conduct regular skydiving operations that sUAS must avoid
P-40 is a Prohibited area where flight by all civil aircraft is not permitted; sUAS may not enter without specific authorization
P-40 is a Positive Control area where all aircraft including sUAS must be on an active ATC clearance at all times
P-40 is a Practice Instrument Approach corridor where IFR training traffic is concentrated at low altitudes

explanations.a: Parachute Jump Zones are depicted with separate symbols and the label 'PARACHUTE JUMPING'; the 'P-' prefix designates a Prohibited area.
explanations.b: On FAA sectional charts, the 'P-' prefix followed by a number designates a Prohibited area — airspace within which no civil aircraft, including sUAS, are permitted without specific authorization from the controlling authority.
explanations.c: Positive Control area is an outdated term; the 'P-' designation specifically denotes a Prohibited area, not a positive control environment.
explanations.d: Practice approach corridors are not depicted with the 'P-' prefix or blue hatching; instrument approach corridors are shown through the depiction of instrument approach procedures, not special use airspace symbols.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.7 Special use airspace summary and identification
questions.keyword: R- restricted area magenta hatch chart identification
questions.text: A remote pilot studying a sectional chart notices a hatched area labeled 'R-4009' with '10000' shown as the ceiling. What type of airspace is this and what does the ceiling indicate?

answers.text: R-4009 is an Alert area with a ceiling of 10,000 ft AGL where military training operations are routinely conducted
R-4009 is a Restricted area with a ceiling of 10,000 ft MSL; entry when active requires authorization from the controlling agency
R-4009 is a Restricted area with a ceiling of 10,000 ft AGL; sUAS may operate at or below 400 ft AGL within the area without restriction
R-4009 is a Warning area with a ceiling of 1,000 ft MSL; civil aircraft may enter freely but must exercise extreme caution

explanations.a: Alert areas use the prefix 'A-', not 'R-'; the 'R-' prefix specifically designates Restricted areas on sectional charts.
explanations.b: The 'R-' prefix designates a Restricted area; the ceiling value on sectional charts for special use airspace is expressed in feet MSL, so 10,000 represents 10,000 ft MSL; entry into an active Restricted area requires authorization from the controlling agency.
explanations.c: While the altitude ceiling is expressed in MSL, not AGL, and sUAS below 400 ft AGL might be far below the ceiling, entry into an active Restricted area still requires authorization regardless of sUAS altitude relative to the ceiling.
explanations.d: Warning areas use the prefix 'W-'; R-4009 is a Restricted area, and the ceiling is MSL not AGL.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: Class G above 1200 AGL 14500 ft MSL en route
questions.text: A remote pilot studying the aeronautical chart legend learns that in some remote western U.S. areas, Class G airspace extends from the surface to 14,500 ft MSL rather than the standard 1,200 ft AGL. What explains the Class G ceiling being 14,500 ft MSL rather than 1,200 ft AGL in these areas?

answers.text: In some western and remote areas lacking standard en route airways, Class E en route airspace begins at 14,500 ft MSL rather than 1,200 ft AGL, leaving a larger Class G band
Class G is extended to 14,500 ft MSL in areas where the terrain exceeds 1,200 ft MSL, ensuring the ceiling remains above mountain peaks
Class G is extended to 14,500 ft in coastal areas to accommodate military seaplane operations that require airspace flexibility below Class E
The FAA designates 14,500 ft Class G ceilings near international borders where radar coverage is limited and positive control is impractical

explanations.a: In certain areas of the western U.S. and other remote regions where Victor airways and Class E transition areas have not been established, Class E en route airspace begins at 14,500 ft MSL instead of the standard 1,200 ft AGL, resulting in a much deeper Class G airspace band below 14,500 ft MSL.
explanations.b: Class G ceiling designation is not based on terrain elevation automatically; the FAA designates specific airspace structures where Class E does not begin until 14,500 ft MSL.
explanations.c: Seaplane operations are not the reason for the higher Class G ceiling; the absence of charted Class E airspace infrastructure explains the elevation.
explanations.d: International border proximity is not the determining factor; the Class G ceiling at 14,500 ft MSL applies in specific unstructured en route areas regardless of border proximity.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: LAANC authorization grid UAS Facility Map participation
questions.text: A remote pilot attempts to use a LAANC-enabled app to get authorization for Class C airspace near an airport. The app indicates the airport is 'not LAANC-participating.' What does this mean for the remote pilot's authorization options?

answers.text: The airport is exempt from Part 107 authorization requirements because non-participating airports have no ATC oversight for sUAS
The remote pilot must contact the tower directly by radio to receive a verbal LAANC clearance through the alternate non-digital pathway
The remote pilot must obtain airspace authorization through the FAA DroneZone manual authorization process, which involves direct ATC facility review
The remote pilot may proceed at any altitude up to 400 ft AGL because non-LAANC airports are automatically designated as Class G below 400 ft AGL

explanations.a: Non-LAANC participation does not exempt the airspace from authorization requirements; Class C airspace still requires ATC authorization under 107.41.
explanations.b: There is no verbal LAANC clearance process via radio; LAANC is exclusively a digital system, and non-participating airports route pilots to the DroneZone manual process.
explanations.c: When an airport or airspace is not part of the LAANC system, the remote pilot must apply for airspace authorization through the FAA DroneZone portal using the manual authorization process, which is reviewed by the applicable ATC facility and may take longer to receive.
explanations.d: Non-LAANC participation does not change the airspace classification; Class C remains controlled airspace requiring authorization regardless of LAANC participation status.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.4 Class D airspace surface area and operating hours
questions.keyword: Class D airspace ceiling 2500 ft above airport elevation
questions.text: A remote pilot is operating near a towered airport whose field elevation is 650 ft MSL. The airport is surrounded by Class D airspace. The remote pilot wants to determine the ceiling of the Class D surface area in MSL terms. What is the approximate Class D ceiling at this airport?

answers.text: 2,500 ft MSL, because Class D airspace always extends to a fixed ceiling of 2,500 ft MSL regardless of airport field elevation
Approximately 3,150 ft MSL, which is 2,500 ft AGL above the airport field elevation of 650 ft MSL
1,200 ft AGL above the airport surface, which equals 1,850 ft MSL for this airport, marking the top of the Class D cylinder
4,000 ft MSL, because all Class D airports are surrounded by airspace extending to the base of Class E en route at 4,000 ft MSL

explanations.a: Class D ceiling is expressed as 2,500 ft above the airport's field elevation (AGL), not a fixed MSL altitude; the MSL equivalent varies with the airport's elevation.
explanations.b: Class D airspace typically extends from the surface to 2,500 ft above the airport field elevation AGL; at an airport with a field elevation of 650 ft MSL, the Class D ceiling is approximately 650 + 2,500 = 3,150 ft MSL, as depicted on the sectional chart.
explanations.c: 1,200 ft AGL is the Class G/E boundary in standard en route areas, not the Class D ceiling; the Class D ceiling is approximately 2,500 ft AGL above the airport.
explanations.d: 4,000 ft MSL is the ceiling for Class C airspace, not Class D; Class D tops at approximately 2,500 ft AGL above the primary airport.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: frequency box underlined CTAF common traffic advisory
questions.text: On a sectional chart, a remote pilot sees '122.8*' next to a non-towered airport frequency box, where the asterisk or underline indicates a specific radio designation. What does the asterisk or underlining of 122.8 indicate about this frequency?

answers.text: 122.8 is the airport's secondary radar surveillance frequency, used to request military flight following services in the area
122.8 is the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF) for that airport, used by pilots to self-announce positions in the traffic pattern
122.8 is a restricted frequency reserved for air carrier operations and may not be monitored by general aviation pilots
122.8 is the Class D clearance delivery frequency for the airport, active only during tower operating hours on weekdays

explanations.a: 122.8 MHz is a widely used CTAF frequency, not a radar or military frequency; radar surveillance uses transponder codes, not a dedicated VHF frequency.
