explanations.b: When a frequency on a sectional chart is underlined or marked with an asterisk (depending on chart edition), it indicates the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF) where pilots flying in and around non-towered airports announce their position and intentions.
explanations.c: 122.8 MHz is a civil aviation frequency open to all pilots; it is not restricted to air carriers.
explanations.d: 122.8 is not a clearance delivery frequency; CTAF is used at non-towered airports for traffic self-announcement, not ATC clearance.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.5 Class E airspace types and floors
questions.keyword: Class E transition area 700 ft AGL IFR departure protection
questions.text: A remote pilot asks an instructor why some non-towered airports have a 700-ft AGL Class E transition area (magenta shading) even though no instrument approaches exist at the airport. The instructor explains the primary purpose of this airspace. Which answer best explains why Class E transition areas exist at some airports?

answers.text: To establish a mandatory fuel stop zone for aircraft operating under instrument flight rules departing or arriving at the airport
To restrict airspace around airports where noise-sensitive communities have requested reduced overflights below 700 ft AGL
To create a buffer zone where all aircraft including sUAS must maintain 500 ft separation from clouds to comply with VFR weather minimums
To provide an area of controlled airspace that protects IFR aircraft transitioning between the instrument environment and the airport traffic area during approaches and departures

explanations.a: Fuel stop requirements are not the purpose of Class E transition areas; this designation is entirely about IFR traffic protection.
explanations.b: Noise abatement is not an airspace classification factor; transition areas are established for air traffic separation purposes, not noise reduction.
explanations.c: While cloud clearance requirements exist in Class E, that is not why transition areas are established; the purpose is IFR traffic containment.
explanations.d: Class E transition areas (depicted by the magenta vignette) exist to contain IFR traffic in controlled airspace as aircraft transition between the en route environment and the airport; this protects instrument approaches and departures from uncontrolled traffic below 700 ft AGL, where the airspace would otherwise be Class G.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.3 Class C airspace dimensions and services
questions.keyword: Class C outer ring 20 nm radius floor 1200 AGL
questions.text: An sUAS remote pilot is operating 12 nautical miles from a Class C primary airport. At this distance, the outer ring of the Class C area has ended, but the remote pilot knows a Class C outer area may still exist. What is the significance of the outer area, and does it create authorization requirements for sUAS?

answers.text: The Class C outer area is an informal advisory zone, not a formally charted airspace class; it creates no authorization requirement for sUAS operations
The Class C outer area extends 20 nm from the primary airport and requires ATC authorization for sUAS just like the core Class C rings
The outer area requires transponder equipment but not ATC authorization; sUAS transponders are prohibited, so sUAS may not enter the outer area
The outer area beyond the charted Class C rings reverts to Class E or Class G depending on altitude; sUAS authorization depends on the actual airspace class at the operating altitude

explanations.a: While the outer area is not formally classified as Class C, the underlying charted airspace (Class E or G) determines the authorization requirement, not the informal outer area concept alone.
explanations.b: The Class C outer area (the informal zone beyond the charted rings) is not a separately authorized airspace class requiring sUAS LAANC authorization; authorization depends on the charted airspace class.
explanations.c: Transponder requirements for manned aircraft in the outer area do not apply to sUAS; Part 107 prohibits transponders on sUAS, and authorization requirements are airspace-class-based.
explanations.d: Beyond the charted Class C rings, the airspace reverts to the underlying classification (typically Class E at 1,200 ft AGL or above and Class G below that); sUAS authorization is determined by this actual charted airspace class, not by the informal outer area concept.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: firefighting TFR 91.137 type I II III applications
questions.text: While checking NOTAMs before a rural sUAS operation, a remote pilot finds a 91.137 TFR in effect over a nearby wildfire. The NOTAM indicates the TFR is a Type I TFR. Which aircraft types are typically permitted within a Type I TFR?

answers.text: All VFR aircraft within 5 nm of the fire perimeter may operate freely because Type I TFRs apply only to IFR aircraft
Only aircraft participating directly in the firefighting operation or those specifically authorized by the controlling agency
Any aircraft below 1,000 ft AGL may transit the TFR because Type I restricts only high-altitude overflights
All aircraft with active ATC flight following are automatically cleared through a Type I TFR without additional authorization

explanations.a: Type I TFRs do not have a VFR exemption at any distance; the restriction applies to all aircraft not authorized by the controlling agency.
explanations.b: A Type I TFR under 14 CFR 91.137(a)(1) is the most restrictive type, permitting entry only to aircraft participating in the firefighting, hazard mitigation, or emergency response activity, plus aircraft authorized by the controlling agency; all other aircraft including sUAS are excluded.
explanations.c: Altitude does not create an exemption within a Type I TFR; the restriction applies throughout the designated altitude block.
explanations.d: ATC flight following provides traffic advisories but does not grant authorization to enter a TFR; specific authorization from the controlling agency is required.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.12 Controlled vs uncontrolled airspace sUAS authorization
questions.keyword: LAANC authorization expiration time window specific
questions.text: A remote pilot obtains a LAANC authorization for a 1-hour window beginning at 10:00 AM in Class D airspace. Due to equipment setup delays, the pilot is unable to launch until 11:15 AM. The LAANC authorization has expired. Under Part 107, what must the pilot do?

answers.text: Proceed with the flight because LAANC authorizations carry a 30-minute grace period for late starts
Fly immediately at or below 50 ft AGL only, which is considered a grace-altitude exemption during authorization gaps
Obtain a new LAANC authorization or DroneZone approval covering the actual intended flight time before launching
Contact the ATC tower by radio to verbally extend the expired LAANC authorization for an additional hour

explanations.a: LAANC authorizations do not carry a 30-minute grace period; the authorization is valid only for the approved time window.
explanations.b: There is no grace-altitude exemption in Part 107 allowing flight below 50 ft AGL on an expired LAANC authorization.
explanations.c: An expired LAANC authorization is no longer valid; the remote pilot must obtain a new authorization covering the actual intended launch time before beginning the flight in controlled airspace.
explanations.d: ATC towers cannot verbally extend LAANC authorizations; the LAANC system and DroneZone portal are the only mechanisms for obtaining or renewing authorization.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.7 Special use airspace summary and identification
questions.keyword: National Security Area voluntary avoidance request
questions.text: A remote pilot notices a shaded area on the sectional chart labeled 'NATIONAL SECURITY AREA' covering a critical infrastructure facility. National Security Areas (NSAs) differ from Restricted and Prohibited areas in how compliance is structured. How does an NSA differ from a Restricted area in terms of pilot obligations?

answers.text: NSAs have the same mandatory prohibition as Restricted areas and require written FAA authorization before any sUAS entry
NSAs require prior notification to DHS via a web portal at least 72 hours before any aircraft enters the designated area
NSAs apply only to manned aircraft above 1,000 ft AGL; sUAS below that altitude are categorically exempt from NSA advisories
NSAs are voluntary avoidance areas where pilots are requested to avoid flight but are not legally prohibited from entry

explanations.a: NSAs do not carry the mandatory legal prohibition of Restricted areas; they are voluntary avoidance areas requesting pilot cooperation rather than prohibiting entry.
explanations.b: There is no DHS web portal notification requirement for NSAs; the pilot is simply requested to voluntarily avoid the area.
explanations.c: NSAs are not limited by aircraft type or altitude; the request to avoid applies to all aircraft, though entry is not prohibited.
explanations.d: National Security Areas established by NOTAM and depicted on charts are voluntary avoidance areas; pilots are requested, not legally required, to avoid flight within NSAs; however, when heightened security warrants, NSAs can be converted to Restricted areas temporarily.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: victor airway V- chart symbol airway width 4 nm each side
questions.text: A remote pilot studying a sectional chart identifies a thin blue line labeled 'V105' running between two VOR stations. The remote pilot wants to know the width of this Victor airway and whether it affects sUAS planning at low altitudes. What are the dimensions of a Victor airway?

answers.text: Victor airways are 2 nautical miles wide total (1 nm each side of centerline) and apply only to IFR traffic above 3,000 ft AGL
Victor airways are 8 nautical miles wide total (4 nm each side of centerline) and extend from 1,200 ft AGL to 17,999 ft MSL
Victor airways are 10 nautical miles wide and extend from the surface to 18,000 ft MSL, requiring sUAS to file a flight plan
Victor airways are 4 nautical miles wide total (2 nm each side of centerline) and extend only in Class B airspace above major hub airports

explanations.a: Victor airways are 8 nm wide, not 2 nm; the 1 nm figure significantly understates the protected width.
explanations.b: Victor airways (Class E en route airways) are 8 nautical miles wide — 4 nm on each side of the centerline — and extend from 1,200 ft AGL (or the Class E floor in that area) to 17,999 ft MSL (the base of Class A); this is relevant context for understanding en route traffic flow.
explanations.c: Victor airways are 8 nm wide, not 10 nm, and they do not require sUAS flight plans; they also do not extend to the surface.
explanations.d: Victor airways span the domestic en route structure and are not limited to Class B airports; they are 8 nm wide, not 4 nm.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: glider activity area airspace awareness hazard
questions.text: While reviewing a sectional chart, a remote pilot sees a symbol and notation indicating 'GLIDER OPERATIONS' in the planned flight area. Although this symbol imposes no regulatory restriction, what is its practical significance for sUAS planning?

answers.text: Glider operations areas are Restricted areas requiring ATC authorization equivalent to Class D before any sUAS may enter

Glider operations areas indicate heightened traffic from unpowered sailplanes that are difficult to detect visually due to their quiet operation and glide profile; remote pilots should increase vigilance for glider traffic
Glider operations are limited to below 200 ft AGL by FAA regulation, so sUAS operating above that altitude are not at risk of conflict
Glider operations symbols indicate areas where sUAS are prohibited from flying because the FAA gives gliders unconditional right of way over all unmanned aircraft

explanations.a: Glider operations areas are not Restricted areas and require no ATC authorization; they are advisory markings to increase pilot awareness.
explanations.b: Glider operations markings on sectional charts indicate areas where unpowered sailplanes are active; gliders are quiet, can achieve significant altitudes, and can be difficult to see; remote pilots should be particularly vigilant for glider traffic in these areas to fulfill see-and-avoid obligations.
explanations.c: Gliders regularly operate well above 200 ft AGL, often achieving altitudes of several thousand feet; the premise that they are limited to 200 ft is incorrect.
explanations.d: Part 107 grants right of way to all manned aircraft over sUAS, not specifically gliders over sUAS; however, gliders have specific right-of-way rules among manned aircraft and are not excluded from Part 107's general manned aircraft right-of-way provision.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.12 Controlled vs uncontrolled airspace sUAS authorization
questions.keyword: LAANC authorization conditions altitude not location
questions.text: A remote pilot receives a LAANC authorization for 200 ft AGL in a Class D airspace grid. During the flight, the pilot wants to climb to 250 ft AGL within the same geographic grid square. The pilot's original LAANC authorization specified 200 ft AGL. Under Part 107, may the pilot climb to 250 ft?

answers.text: Yes, because LAANC authorizations cover the entire 400 ft AGL operational envelope within the authorized grid square
No, but the pilot may verbally inform the tower of the altitude change by radio, which constitutes an automatic authorization amendment
No, the LAANC authorization is specific to the altitude ceiling approved; operating above 200 ft AGL without a new authorization would violate the terms of the airspace authorization
Yes, provided no manned aircraft are observed in the vicinity and VLOS of the sUAS is maintained at the higher altitude

explanations.a: LAANC authorizations grant access up to the specific altitude approved, not automatically to 400 ft AGL; exceeding the authorized ceiling violates the authorization.
explanations.b: Radio notification to the tower does not amend a LAANC authorization; a new LAANC request or DroneZone authorization is required for the higher altitude.
explanations.c: A LAANC authorization is altitude-specific; the approved ceiling of 200 ft AGL is the maximum for that authorization, and climbing to 250 ft AGL without a revised authorization for a higher ceiling exceeds the approved parameters.
explanations.d: Absence of nearby manned aircraft and maintaining VLOS do not expand the scope of an airspace authorization; the approved altitude ceiling must be respected.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.5 Class E airspace types and floors
questions.keyword: Federal airways Class E 18000 ft MSL boundary Class A
questions.text: A remote pilot wants to understand the upper boundary of Class E airspace in the domestic en route environment. Where does Class E airspace end vertically in the contiguous U.S. en route environment, and what airspace begins immediately above it?

answers.text: Class E ends at 12,500 ft MSL, above which positive control by ATC is maintained through Class A procedures for all aircraft
Class E ends at 17,999 ft MSL, above which Class A airspace begins at 18,000 ft MSL extending to FL600
Class E ends at 14,500 ft MSL where offshore Alert areas begin over the continental shelf of the Atlantic coast
Class E has no defined upper ceiling; it merges with Class A airspace without a defined boundary point

explanations.a: Class E does not end at 12,500 ft MSL; that altitude is relevant to certain VFR cruising altitude and oxygen requirements, not Class E boundaries.
explanations.b: In the contiguous U.S. en route environment, Class E airspace extends from its floor (1,200 ft AGL, 700 ft AGL, or the surface as designated) up to but not including 18,000 ft MSL — that is, to 17,999 ft MSL — where Class A airspace begins at 18,000 ft MSL (FL180).
explanations.c: 14,500 ft MSL is a Class E floor in certain remote western areas, not an upper boundary related to Alert areas; 17,999 ft MSL is the correct upper limit.
explanations.d: Class E does have a defined upper boundary at 17,999 ft MSL; it does not merge with Class A without demarcation.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: TFR VIP movement NOTAM preflight check required
questions.text: A remote pilot checks NOTAMs the evening before a scheduled flight and finds no active TFRs. On the day of the flight, a last-minute presidential visit to the city creates a new TFR that covers the planned flight area. The pilot has already arrived at the launch site without rechecking NOTAMs. Under Part 107, how should the pilot handle this situation?

answers.text: Proceed with the flight because the TFR was issued after the pilot's last NOTAM check, which occurred at a reasonable time before the flight
Check NOTAMs again before launch; if a new TFR now covers the flight area, do not fly until the TFR expires or a relief is obtained
Fly only below 100 ft AGL, which is below the floor of all presidential TFRs and therefore legal without rechecking NOTAMs
Contact the nearest ATC facility by radio from the launch site to request a verbal TFR status check before launch

explanations.a: Prior NOTAM checks do not satisfy the preflight obligation if sufficient time has passed for new TFRs to be issued; TFRs can be activated with very short notice, particularly for security events.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.49, the remote PIC must familiarize themselves with all relevant information before each flight; TFRs can be issued with short notice and the pilot's preflight NOTAM check must occur as close to the launch time as practicable — discovering a new TFR means the flight cannot proceed without authorization.
explanations.c: Presidential TFRs begin at the surface; there is no 100-ft AGL floor exemption in a presidential TFR.
explanations.d: While contacting ATC for TFR status is a reasonable step, the definitive source is the official NOTAM system; radio contact is supplementary, not the primary compliance method.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: parachute jump area symbol sectional chart hazard
questions.text: During preflight chart review, a remote pilot spots the symbol for a parachute jump area overlapping the planned flight path at approximately 3,000 ft AGL. Since sUAS are limited to 400 ft AGL, does the parachute jump area pose any hazard or concern for the remote pilot?

answers.text: No, because parachutists only operate above 2,500 ft AGL and sUAS never reach those altitudes under Part 107 standard rules
Yes, parachutists in freefall and under canopy can descend rapidly through all altitudes including the 0–400 ft AGL operating band, posing a collision hazard
No, parachute jump areas carry a legal prohibition preventing any parachutist from descending below 500 ft AGL in the designated drop zone
No, parachute jump areas are only active on weekends and holidays, and sUAS may always operate there on weekdays without concern

explanations.a: Parachutists descend through all altitudes from their exit point all the way to the ground; they do not remain exclusively above 2,500 ft AGL.
explanations.b: Parachutists exit aircraft at altitude and descend under gravity and canopy through all altitude bands including 0 to 400 ft AGL; a remote pilot operating within or near a parachute drop zone must be aware that parachutists can appear at any altitude, including the sUAS operating band.
explanations.c: There is no regulatory floor of 500 ft AGL for parachutists; they land on the ground and pass through all altitudes in the drop zone.
explanations.d: Parachute jump areas can be active any day of the week and are not limited to weekends; the sectional chart symbol indicates a regularly used drop zone requiring ongoing awareness.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.2 Class B airspace structure and sUAS authorization requirement
questions.keyword: Class B inner ring surface VFR flight visibility requirement
questions.text: A remote pilot with LAANC authorization to fly in the inner ring of Class B airspace must also comply with weather minimums applicable to the airspace. What are the Part 91 VFR weather minimums applicable to aircraft (including sUAS by analogy) operating within Class B airspace?

answers.text: 3 statute miles visibility and clear of clouds; Class B is defined by radar separation, not cloud distance requirements
5 statute miles visibility and clear of clouds, with no specific cloud distance required in Class B
3 statute miles visibility and 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds
1 statute mile visibility with no cloud clearance required because Class B is always operated under IFR regardless of VMC conditions

explanations.a: In Class B airspace, the VFR weather minimum under 14 CFR 91.155 is 3 statute miles flight visibility and clear of clouds; because ATC provides separation from other aircraft in Class B, specific cloud distance requirements are not mandated.
explanations.b: 5 statute miles is more than required in Class B; the VFR visibility minimum in Class B is 3 statute miles.
explanations.c: The 500/1,000/2,000 cloud clearances apply in Class C, D, and Class E airspace below 10,000 ft MSL, not in Class B; Class B has its own, simpler weather minimums.
explanations.d: 1 statute mile visibility is less than the 3 SM minimum; Class B is positive-controlled airspace where ATC provides IFR/VFR separation, but the weather minimums still apply to VFR pilots.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: airport traffic area vs surface area distinction
questions.text: A remote pilot studying ground school asks about the difference between an airport traffic area and an airport surface area in the context of current U.S. airspace classification. Which statement accurately addresses this distinction?

answers.text: Airport traffic area is a current official airspace classification extending 5 miles from a towered airport and requiring ATC authorization for all aircraft
Airport traffic area was a pre-1993 airspace concept that no longer exists as an official designation; modern U.S. airspace uses the B/C/D/E/G classification system
Airport traffic area and surface area are two names for the same airspace class used interchangeably in Part 107 publications
Airport traffic area refers to the control zone around a towered airport while the surface area refers to the runway environment within airport property boundaries

explanations.a: Airport traffic area is not a current official FAA airspace classification; it was replaced by the current B/C/D/E/G system effective September 1993.
explanations.b: The airport traffic area (ATA) was an airspace concept used before the 1993 reclassification of U.S. airspace to the current ICAO-aligned Class A through G system; it no longer exists as an official designation and should not be confused with current airspace classes.
explanations.c: Airport traffic area and surface area are not interchangeable; surface area is a component of current Class B, C, D, and E surface designations, while airport traffic area is an obsolete term.
explanations.d: These are not two names for the same concepts in current FAA airspace classification; the ATA predates the current system and the surface area is a specific type designation within modern controlled airspace classes.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.keyword: controlled airspace notation SFC notation surface Class E
questions.text: On a sectional chart, an area is labeled with a blue-outlined region and the notation 'SFC-4000' within it. What does this notation indicate about the airspace classification in that shaded region?

answers.text: The airspace is a Class E surface area extending from the surface to 4,000 ft MSL, likely associated with an approach corridor or Class E extension
The airspace is Class G from the surface to 4,000 ft MSL; sUAS may operate freely throughout this band without ATC authorization
The notation indicates a Restricted area from the surface to 4,000 ft MSL where all aircraft require written authorization
The notation indicates a Class B shelf with the floor at the surface and the ceiling at 4,000 ft MSL requiring ATC authorization for sUAS

explanations.a: Airspace notations showing 'SFC-xxxx' in a Class E context indicate the airspace begins at the surface and extends to the listed altitude MSL; this format commonly appears in Class E surface extensions associated with instrument approach corridors, requiring ATC authorization for sUAS under 107.41.
explanations.b: SFC-4000 in a controlled airspace context does not indicate Class G; Class G is uncontrolled and typically not labeled with altitude ceilings in this format.
explanations.c: Restricted areas use the 'R-' prefix notation, not a 'SFC-xxxx' label; the SFC notation without an R prefix indicates a Class E surface area, not a Restricted area.
explanations.d: While Class B also uses altitude range notation and requires ATC authorization, Class B is depicted with solid blue lines and concentric rings, not a simple SFC-4000 label box common in Class E surface area extensions.

questions.name: Airspace Classification and Operational Requirements
questions.objective: 4.12 Controlled vs uncontrolled airspace sUAS authorization
questions.keyword: multiple airspace classes stacked at same location altitude determines class
questions.text: A remote pilot operates directly beneath a Class C outer ring whose floor is charted at 1,200 ft MSL, at an altitude of 300 ft AGL over terrain that sits at 850 ft MSL. The remote pilot is therefore at approximately 1,150 ft MSL. What airspace class applies to this operation?

answers.text: Class C, because the operation occurs beneath the outer ring of Class C airspace and sUAS are subject to its requirements regardless of actual MSL altitude
Class E, because all areas beneath Class C outer rings are automatically designated Class E from 700 ft AGL upward
Class G, because the aircraft at 1,150 ft MSL is below the Class C floor of 1,200 ft MSL and any non-surface Class E floor at 1,200 ft AGL would be even higher
Class D, because any aircraft operating below a Class C ring defaults to Class D airspace classification pending ATC coordination

explanations.a: The aircraft at 1,150 ft MSL is below the Class C outer ring floor of 1,200 ft MSL; it is not within Class C airspace and its associated requirements do not apply.
explanations.b: Class E does not automatically begin at 700 ft AGL beneath Class C rings; the underlying airspace depends on what is charted, and in many cases it is Class G below the Class C floor.
explanations.c: If the Class C floor is 1,200 ft MSL and the aircraft is at 1,150 ft MSL, the aircraft is below the Class C floor; absent a charted Class E surface area or transition area at that location, the airspace below the Class C floor is Class G (or non-surface Class E beginning at 1,200 ft AGL if so charted); regardless, the aircraft is not in Class C and no Class C authorization is needed.
explanations.d: There is no regulatory principle causing airspace to default to Class D beneath Class C layers; airspace classification is fixed by FAA designation, not by aircraft relative position to other airspace classes.
